About: The Rolling Race — Only the Shape Decides

Source

Topic
Rigid body rolling motion on an incline (NCERT Class 11, Ch. 6 — Systems of Particles & Rotational Motion)
Concept
For a body rolling without slipping down an incline, a = g·sinθ/(1 + I/MR²); the finishing order depends ONLY on the shape factor I/MR², not on mass or radius.
Serves
Moment of inertia as shape geometry; the rolling constraint ω = v/r; energy sharing between translation and rotation; a target JEE result.
Inquiry
What decides who wins the race — mass, radius, or shape?
Misconception
"The heaviest one wins" / "the biggest one wins." Neither M nor R appears in a — they cancel out.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Predict the winner

A solid sphere, a solid disc and a thin hoop — same mass, same radius — are released together from the top of an incline. They roll without slipping. Which one reaches the finish line first?

2 · Watch the race

Press ▶ Play. Watch the sphere pull steadily away from the disc, and the disc from the hoop. Look at each body's I/MR² in the sidebar — that single number is doing all the work.

3 · The misconception test

If you change the Mass & Radius slider, the bodies grow heavier and larger on screen. What do you predict happens to the finishing order?

4 · The whole result

The acceleration of a body rolling without slipping is

a = g·sinθ / (1 + I/MR²)

Mass and radius appear nowhere. Only the shape factor I/MR² — 0.4 for the solid sphere, 0.5 for the disc, 1 for the thin hoop — decides who wins. Now try the Mass & Radius slider — every I/MR² stays put — or move the incline to change how fast the race runs. Turn on ∑ Formal for the derivation.

The Physics

The Rolling Race — Only the Shape Decides · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Three bodies of different shape start together at the top of an incline and roll down to the FINISH line at its foot. You can tilt the slope and rescale the bodies to find out what controls how fast a rolling body goes.

What you'll learn

  • How rolling without slipping ties a body's spinning to its forward motion.
  • What the shape factor I/MR² measures, and where it enters the acceleration down a slope.
  • Which of the incline angle, the mass and the radius the acceleration depends on.
The apparatus: three bodies released together from rest at START, rolling a ramp of length L to the FINISH line.

What's on screen

  • Incline with the angle θ, a START mark, a dashed FINISH line, and the ramp length L = 2.0 m.
  • Solid sphere (blue) and solid disc (pink), drawn with spokes that turn as they roll.
  • Thin hoop (yellow): a ring with one spoke.
  • Shape factor panel in the sidebar, one I/MR² number per body, and the t clock showing time since release.
See itLook at the apparatus at the start of a run. Watch for: the three bodies stacked at START, the angle θ at the foot of the ramp, and the dashed FINISH line.

03

Rolling without slipping ties the spin to the motion

A body rolls without slipping when the point touching the ramp is momentarily at rest. Then the speed of its centre and its spin are tied together:

v = ωR,   a = αR
R is the radius. ω and α are the angular speed and angular acceleration about the centre.

Two forces act along the slope: the pull Mg sinθ of gravity, and static friction f at the contact point, pointing up the slope. Friction does two jobs:

  • its torque about the centre spins the body up: fR = Iα;
  • it cuts the net force along the slope: Mg sinθ − f = Ma.

The contact point does not slide, so friction does no work. It moves energy between spinning and moving but removes none.

Forces on the body (slope drawn descending to the right). The normal force N balances the part Mg cosθ of the weight.
See itRun the race at 30°. Watch for: each body turning as it moves down the ramp, the spokes and white dot going round with no sliding.
04

The shape factor I/MR² is a pure number

The moment of inertia I measures how hard it is to change a body's spin. For mass M and radius R it can always be written

I = c MR²
c = I/MR² depends only on how the mass is spread, about the axis through the centre.
BodyIc = I/MR²
Solid sphere⅖ MR²0.400
Solid disc½ MR²0.500
Thin hoopMR²1.000

The nearer the mass sits to the axis, the smaller c is; in a thin hoop all of it is at distance R. Doubling M or doubling R changes I and MR² by the same factor, so their ratio does not move. The panel keeps reading 0.400, 0.500 and 1.000 at every setting of the Mass & radius slider.

See itSet Mass & radius to 3.0×. Watch for: the three I/MR² numbers unchanged at 0.400, 0.500 and 1.000, though the bodies are drawn much larger.
05

The acceleration down the slope is g sinθ / (1 + I/MR²)

Put fR = Iα and a = Rα together: f = Ia/R² = cMa. Then Mg sinθ − f = Ma becomes Mg sinθ = M(1 + c)a, so

a = g sinθ / (1 + I/MR²)
M and R have cancelled. Only g, θ and the shape factor remain.

A block sliding without friction would have a = g sinθ, which is the case c = 0. Every rolling body is slower, because part of the pull goes into spinning it. From rest over the ramp length L, t = √(2L/a). At 30° with L = 2.0 m:

Bodya (m/s²)time to FINISH
Solid sphere3.501.07 s
Solid disc3.271.11 s
Thin hoop2.451.28 s
See itRun the race at 30° and wait for all three. Watch for: the sphere, then the disc, then the hoop reaching FINISH, and the t clock stopping near 1.28 s.
06

Energy gives the same result

Friction does no work here, so the drop in height h turns entirely into kinetic energy, shared between moving and spinning. With ω = v/R and I = cMR²:

Mgh = ½Mv² + ½Iω² = ½Mv²(1 + c)
So v² = 2gh/(1 + c).

At 30° the ramp drops h = L sinθ = 1.0 m, giving 3.74 m/s for the sphere, 3.62 m/s for the disc and 3.13 m/s for the hoop at FINISH. These agree with v² = 2aL from the previous section.

The share of the energy that goes into spin is c/(1 + c): 2/7 for the sphere, 1/3 for the disc and 1/2 for the hoop. The larger that share, the less energy is left for motion along the slope.

07

What changes the pace: the angle and the shape, not M or R

  • Mass and radius. They cancel in a, so the slider changes the bodies' size on screen and the M and R used in the sim, but not the accelerations, the times or the finishing order.
  • Angle. It enters only through sinθ. A steeper ramp raises all three accelerations in the same proportion, so every body arrives sooner and the order does not change.
  • Shape. The ratios between bodies stay fixed: disc/sphere = 1.4/1.5 ≈ 0.93 and hoop/sphere = 1.4/2 = 0.70, at any angle.

The hoop needs 2.17 s at 10° and 0.97 s at 60°. The sphere needs 1.81 s and 0.81 s.

See itRace at 30° with Mass & radius at 3.0×. Watch for: the same finishing order and the t clock stopping near 1.28 s again, with the bodies drawn much larger.
See itRace on the steepest ramp, 60°. Watch for: all three arriving sooner, in the same order, with the t clock stopping near 0.97 s.
08

Where it matters

  • Ramp races. A solid cylinder (c = ½) beats a thin-walled pipe (c ≈ 1) down the same ramp, a standard lab demonstration of moment of inertia.
  • Galileo's ramps. Rolling a solid ball down a gentle ramp slows the motion enough to measure it, and the ball's acceleration is 5/7 of g sinθ.
  • Flywheels. For the same mass and speed, a rim-heavy wheel (c near 1) stores more spin energy ½Iω² than a solid one, so flywheels carry their mass at the rim.
Go deeper

The same method works for any shape: a hollow sphere has c = ⅔, so a = 0.6 g sinθ. Static friction supplies f = c Mg sinθ/(1 + c), which must not exceed μsMg cosθ. That needs μs ≥ c tanθ/(1 + c), and the sim assumes it holds: the hoop at 60° would need μs ≥ 0.87.

09

Summary

In one line. A body rolling down an incline without slipping has its speed and its spin tied together, and this sim compares three shapes to show what sets the pace.

Key points

  • Rolling without slipping gives a = g sinθ / (1 + I/MR²), where I/MR² = c is set by shape alone.
  • Mass and radius cancel; the angle enters only through sinθ.
  • In energy terms v² = 2gh/(1 + c), and the share c/(1 + c) of the energy goes into spin.

Common mix-ups

  • "The heavier or bigger body rolls down faster." M and R cancel out of a, so size and mass do not change the pace.
  • "Friction wastes energy as the body rolls." With no slipping, friction does no work. It only shifts energy between spinning and moving.
  • "A rolling body goes down as fast as a sliding one." The rolling acceleration is g sinθ divided by (1 + c), always smaller than the frictionless sliding value.

Things to try on your own

  • At 45°, use t = √(2L/a) to predict the hoop's time, then run the race and read the t clock.
  • Find the angle at which the sphere takes about as long as the hoop does at 60°.
  • At 20°, work out how far behind the sphere the disc is when the sphere finishes.
